body.en: A singly linked list is a chain of *nodes*. Each node holds data and a reference (link) to the next node; the last node's link is null. A reference called start (or head) points to the first node. In Java: class Node { int data; Node next; Node(int d) { data = d; next = null; } }. Because nodes are created with new as needed, the list grows and shrinks at run time (dynamic memory), and nodes need not be next to each other in memory.

body.en: Arrays give direct access by index in one step but have a fixed size, and inserting or deleting in the middle shifts elements. *Linked lists* grow and shrink freely and insert or delete with a few link changes once the position is found, but must be traversed from start to reach a node (no random access), and each node uses extra memory for its link. Variations: doubly linked lists (links both ways) and circular lists (last node links to the first).
